topics.title: Chapter 57 — Memory-Safety Vulnerabilities
topics.summary: A memory-safety vulnerability arises when a program permits access outside the intended bounds, lifetime, type, or ownership of an object in a way that can affect security. The underlying mistake may begin as an ordinary correctness bug, but untrusted input can make its consequences repeatable and externally controllable. The defensive objective is to prevent invalid operations before they occur. Page permissions and hardening features are valuable secondary barriers, but they do not replace length validation, checked arithmetic, lifetime management, and synchronization. This chapter uses safe rejection tests rather than exploitation exercises. [ R5 , R8 , R34 ]

topics.title: 57.1 Buffer overflows
topics.summary: A buffer overflow writes beyond a buffer’s valid extent. The immediate cause can be an unchecked length, a missing terminator allowance, a wrong element-size calculation, or a parser that trusts a field before validating it. Tie every byte operation to an explicit extent. For a destination of capacity c and requested copy length n , prove n <= c before copying. For a string requiring a terminator, include that byte in the contract without computing an overflowing n + 1 . A length-aware interface helps, but its supplied lengths must still be correct.

topics.title: 57.2 Stack corruption
topics.summary: Stack corruption damages automatic storage or implementation-managed call state. A write beyond a local array can affect nearby objects, saved registers, or other control information depending on layout and optimization. Do not rely on a particular stack arrangement to decide whether an overflow is harmless. Compilers can reorder, eliminate, or place objects differently. Prevent the out-of-bounds write itself; a test that happens to modify only padding on one build does not establish safety.

topics.title: 57.3 Heap corruption
topics.summary: Heap corruption damages dynamically allocated objects or allocator bookkeeping. A write can remain inside a mapped writable page and still cross an allocation boundary. The operating system’s page checks may therefore permit the machine access while the language program has already violated its contract. Allocator crashes often occur later than the original bad write. A failure during allocation or deallocation may be a symptom of earlier corruption, not proof that the allocator is the root cause. Instrumented testing and minimizing the first invalid operation are more useful than patching the eventual crash site blindly.

topics.title: 57.4 Use-after-free
topics.summary: Use-after-free accesses an object after its lifetime and ownership have ended. The address may still be mapped and may even contain plausible data. Reuse by another allocation can turn the stale access into corruption of an unrelated object. Ownership abstractions reduce the risk, but raw observers still need lifetime rules. A unique_ptr prevents duplicate ownership but does not make every raw pointer derived from it safe after reset. Shared ownership can extend lifetime, but it does not automatically synchronize mutable contents.

topics.title: 57.5 Integer errors
topics.summary: Integer errors can create memory vulnerabilities indirectly. A negative length converted to an unsigned size can become very large. A wrapped multiplication can allocate too little storage for a later copy. A truncating conversion can make validation inspect a different value from the one subsequently used. Validate in a representation that can express the required range, then convert. For allocation size count * element_size , require count <= maximum / element_size when the element size is nonzero. Use the same validated value for the actual operation; re-parsing or recomputing with different types can reintroduce the defect.

LECTURE NARRATION
A memory-safety vulnerability arises when a program permits access outside the intended bounds, lifetime, type, or ownership of an object in a way that can affect security. The underlying mistake may begin as an ordinary correctness bug, but untrusted input can make its consequences repeatable and externally controllable. The defensive objective is to prevent invalid operations before they occur. Page permissions and hardening features are valuable secondary barriers, but they do not replace length validation, checked arithmetic, lifetime management, and synchronization.
